<!-- customthm-1: body_md -->
{A}[Theorem \ref{thm:RH_main}, Corollary \ref{cor:other_bases}]
Consider $(\X,\mathcal{M}_\@undefined)$ with $\X$ smooth and quasicompact over $\Spf \W(k)$ as above. There is a symmetric monoidal equivalence
\[\T_\ensuremath{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}: \@undefined_{\mathrm{fgu}}((\X,\mathcal{M}_\@undefined)_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}, \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}[1/\I_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}]_p^{\wedge})^{\op} \longrightarrow \@undefined^{(b),\mathrm{pKum}}_{\cons,\@undefined}((\X,\mathcal{M}_\@undefined)_{\eta},\Z_p)\]
where the target consists of the $p$-Kummer complexes in  $\@undefined^{(b)}_{\cons,\@undefined}((\X,\mathcal{M}_{\@undefined})_\eta,\Z_p)$. If $\X_\eta$ is pure of dimension $d$, then $\T_\ensuremath{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}[d]$ identifies the standard $t$-structure on the source with the $p^+$-perverse $t$-structure on the target.
\label{thm:main_introduction}
<!-- end customthm-1 -->
<!-- customthm-2: body_md -->
{B}[Variant of Theorem \ref{thm:qdR_crys_Gamma_mod}]
\label{thm:local_introduction}
Let $(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})$ be a framed log affine, with framing denoted by $\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}$. Evaluation on the log $q$-de Rham prism $(\R^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\llbracket q-1 \rrbracket, [p]_q, \N^r)^a$ over $\R$ induces an equivalence
\[\@undefined_{\mathrm{fgu}}((\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}, \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}[1/\I_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}]_p^{\wedge}) \simeq \@undefined_{\mathrm{fgu}}(\R^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\mathopen{(\mkern-3mu(}q-1\mathclose{)\mkern-3mu)}^{\wedge}_p)^{h\Gamma},\]
where $(a,b_1,\ldots, b_n)\in \Gamma=\Z_p^\times \ltimes \Z_p(1)^n$ acts by $q\mapsto q^a$ and $\T_i\mapsto q^{pb_i}\T_i$, and ``fgu'' or finitely generated unit means that the complex has a unit Frobenius and is perfect over $\R^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\mathopen{(\mkern-3mu(}q-1\mathclose{)\mkern-3mu)}^{\wedge}_p\langle \mathrm{F}\rangle$.
<!-- end customthm-2 -->
<!-- customthm-3: body_md -->
{C}[Theorem \ref{thm:fgu_pushforward_compat}]
Let $f:(\X,\mathcal{M})\to(\Y,\mathcal{N})$ be a strict log smooth proper morphism of pure relative dimension $d$ between smooth quasicompact $p$-adic formal schemes over $\W(k)[\zeta_{p^\ell}]$ for some $\ell\geq0$, and let $\@undefined_\X$ and $\@undefined_\Y$ be horizontal normal crossings divisors inducing $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$. Suppose the adic generic fibers have pure dimensions $d_\X$ and $d_\Y$. Then there is a commutative diagram
\begin{display}
\@undefined_{\mathrm{fgu}}((\X,\mathcal{M})_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}, \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}[1/\I_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}]_p^{\wedge})^\op \ar{r}{\T_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}},\X}[d_\X]} \ar{d}{\R f_* \{d\} [d]} & \@undefined^{(b)}_{\cons,\@undefined_\X}((\X,\mathcal{M})_\eta,\Z_p) \ar{d}{\R f_{\eta,*}} \\
\@undefined_{\mathrm{fgu}}((\Y,\mathcal{N})_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}, \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}[1/\I_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}]_p^{\wedge})^\op \ar{r}{\T_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}},\Y}[d_\Y]} & \@undefined^{(b)}_{\cons,\@undefined_\Y}((\Y,\mathcal{N})_\eta,\Z_p).
\end{display}
<!-- end customthm-3 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
All categories are $\infty$-categories, unless otherwise stated. We will generally assume $\X$ is a smooth quasicompact $p$-adic formal scheme over $\Spf\W(k)[\zeta_{p^\ell}]$, $\ell\geq0$, with log structure $\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}_\@undefined$ induced by a horizontal normal crossings divisor $\@undefined$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:katz}
Let $\R$ be a perfect $\F_p$-algebra. Then there is an equivalence of categories
\[\Perf(\W(\R))^{\varphi=1} \simeq \@undefined^{(b)}_{\mathrm{lisse}}(\Spec \R, \Z_p),\]
induced by the solution functor
\[\M\longmapsto\left(\M\otimes_{\W(\R)}\W(\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\Spec\R,\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}})\right)^{\varphi=1}.\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We apply Lemma \ref{lem:categorical_nakayama}, which is a variant of derived Nakayama for categories that we will use frequently (and prove shortly).

The hypotheses of this lemma ask that both source and target can be written as $\N$-indexed limits of idempotent complete $\Z_p$-linear categories. For the source we use $\Perf(\W_n(\R))^{\varphi=1}$ and for the target we use $\@undefined^{(b)}_{\mathrm{lisse}}(\Spec \R, \Z/p^n)$ (we impose a Tor boundedness condition now). It is easy to check idempotent completeness here since both sit in ambient idempotent complete categories and their defining conditions are closed under retracts. 

Finally, the reduction modulo $p$ becomes \cite[Proposition 3.4]{BhattScholzePrismaticFCrystals}. Thus by Lemma \ref{lem:categorical_nakayama} the desired claim follows.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:katz_contra}
The Emerton-Kisin correspondence is contravariant. Since $\Perf$ is self-dual, the previous correspondence also admits a dual or contravariant version. The solution functor is $\M \mapsto \underline{\mathrm{RHom}}_{\Perf^{\varphi}(\W(\R)_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}})}(\M_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}, \W(\R)_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}})$ (regarded as a pro\'{e}tale sheaf). Similarly other correspondences reducing to Katz's theorem, such as \cite[Corollary 3.7]{BhattScholzePrismaticFCrystals} or \cite{KoshikawaYaoCorrigendum} admit contravariant versions.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an idempotent complete $\Perf(\Z_p)$-linear stable $\infty$-category. Write 
\[\mathcal{C}_n:=\mathcal{C}\otimes_{\Perf(\Z_p)}\Perf(\Z/p^n).\]
We say that $\mathcal{C}$ is derived $p$-complete if the natural functor $\mathcal{C}\to\varprojlim_n\mathcal{C}_n$ is an equivalence.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{C} = \lim \mathcal{C}_n$ and $\mathcal{D} = \lim \mathcal{D}_n$ be derived $p$-complete idempotent complete categories as in the previous setup. Consider an exact functor
\[\mathrm{F}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}\]
induced by a compatible system $\{\mathrm{F}_n\}$ of functors $\mathcal{C}_n \to \mathcal{D}_n$.

If $\mathrm{F}_1$ is an equivalence, then $\mathrm{F}$ is an equivalence.
\label{lem:categorical_nakayama}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Full faithfulness reduces to the ordinary derived Nakayama lemma. Indeed,
\[\RHom_{\mathcal{C}_1}(\X_1,\Y_1)\simeq \RHom_{\mathcal{C}}(\X,\Y\mathord{/\mkern-6mu/} p) \simeq \RHom_{\mathcal{C}}(\X,\Y) \otimes_{\Z_p}^{\mathrm{L}} \F_p.\]
Note that by our setup $\RHom_{\mathcal{C}}(\X,\Y)$ is derived $p$-complete. Similarly one also gets full faithfulness of $\mathrm{F}_n$.

For essential surjectivity, we observe that $\mathrm{F}$ is exact and fully faithful. The essential image will be a thick subcategory of the target $\mathcal{D}$ using idempotent completeness of $\mathcal{C}$; in fact the same is true for each $\mathrm{F}_n$ (this point is why we impose idempotent completeness).

Thus we can consider the Verdier quotient
\[\mathcal{Q} = \cofib(\mathrm{F})\]
where cofibers are taken in $\mathsf{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{\Z_p}$. Set also $\mathcal{Q}_n = \cofib(\mathrm{F}_n)$, although a priori it need not be the case $\mathcal{Q}=\lim_n \mathcal{Q}_n$ (and we will not need this).

It will suffice to show each $\mathcal{Q}_n = \mathcal{Q}\otimes_{\Perf(\Z_p)} \Perf(\Z/p^n)$ is zero, using the fact that $\mathcal{Q}_1$ is zero. Because we showed that the essential image in $\mathcal{D}_n$ is thick, this is enough to show essential surjectivity for each $n$ and hence for $\mathrm{F}$. Otherwise, we would only deduce that $\mathrm{F}_n(\mathcal{C}_n)$ generates $\mathcal{D}_n$.

Considering some $\M \in \mathcal{Q}$, observe that
\[\cofib(p \cdot \id_{\M}) = \M \otimes^{\mathrm{L}}_{\Z_p} \Z/p\Z.\]
But there is an adjunction $\mathrm{red}_1 \leftrightarrows \mathrm{for}_1$ for the reduction functor $\mathrm{red}_1: \mathcal{Q} \to \mathcal{Q}_1$ (the right adjoint being forgetful), which has the property that $\mathrm{for}_1 \mathrm{red}_1$ recovers $- \otimes_{\Z_p} \Z/p\Z$. Since in this case $\mathrm{red}_1$ is zero we conclude that $\cofib(p \cdot \id_{\M})$ is zero. 

Thus $p$ acts invertibly on $\mathcal{Q}$ and therefore each $\mathcal{Q}_n$, which can only be the case if each $\mathcal{Q}_n$ is the zero category. The claim then follows.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
We use $({}^p\@undefined^{\leq0},{}^p\@undefined^{\geq0})$ to denote Gabber's perverse $t$-structure on $\@undefined^{(b)}_{\mathrm{cons}}(\X,\Z_p)$, and write ${}^p\mathrm{H}^i$ for perverse cohomology sheaves.

We may then construct the $p^+$-perverse $t$-structure, specified by
\[{}^{p^+}\@undefined^{\leq0}=\{\mathscr{F}\in{}^p\@undefined^{\leq1}\mid{}^p\mathrm{H}^1(\mathscr{F})\text{ is locally bounded }p\text{-power torsion}\},\]
\[{}^{p^+}\@undefined^{\geq0}=\{\mathscr{F}\mid \mathscr{F}\mathord{/\mkern-6mu/} p\in{}^p\@undefined^{\geq0}(\X_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}},\F_p)\}.\]
For every $n\geq1$, derived reduction modulo $p^n$ is left $t$-exact for $p^+$-perversity. Moreover, $\mathscr{F}\in{}^{p^+}\@undefined^{\geq0}$ if and only if $\mathscr{F}\mathord{/\mkern-6mu/} p\in{}^p\@undefined^{\geq0}(\X_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}},\F_p)$. This is similar in spirit to \cite[Construction 4.3 and Proposition 4.6]{BhattHansenCons}.
\label{def:EK_pplus}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathscr{X}/\Spf \W(k)$ be smooth and quasicompact. Then there is an equivalence
\[\mathrm{RSol}: \@undefined^{b}_{\fgu}(\@undefined_{\mathrm{F},\mathscr{X}})^\op \simeq \@undefined^{b}_{\mathrm{cons}}(\X, \Z_p),\]
where $\X=\mathscr{X}_{p=0}$. Explicitly, the functor is given by 
\[\mathrm{RSol}_{\X}(\M) = \underline{\mathrm{RHom}}_{\@undefined_{\mathrm{F},\mathscr{X}_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}}}}(\M_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}, \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathscr{X},\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}}) \in \@undefined(\X_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}},\Z_p).\]
If $\X$ is pure of dimension $d$, then $\mathrm{RSol}_{\X}[d]$ identifies the standard $t$-structure on the source with the $p^+$-perverse $t$-structure on the target.
\label{thm:EK_formal_lift}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We first note that one has
\[\@undefined^{b}_{\fgu}(\@undefined_{\mathrm{F},\mathscr{X}}) \simeq \lim_n\@undefined^{b}_{\fgu,\mathrm{tf}}(\@undefined_{\mathrm{F},\mathscr{X}_{p^n=0}})\]
and similarly
\[\@undefined^{b}_{\cons}(\X,\Z_p) \simeq \lim_n\@undefined^{b}_{\mathrm{cons}}(\X_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}},\Z/p^n) = \lim_n \@undefined^{b}_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\X_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}},\Z/p^n).\]
Here $\mathrm{tf}$ means Tor finite. The second equivalence follows from \cite[Theorem 1.6(2)]{HemoRicharzScholbach2023}, and their Remark 7.2 to identify with $\@undefined^{b}_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\X_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}},\Z/p^n)$.

Because each side here sits in an obvious ambient category that is idempotent complete and the imposed conditions are stable under retracts, we get the idempotent completeness requirement for Lemma \ref{lem:categorical_nakayama}. It is straightforward to show that the categories we have written here in each limit are obtained by applying $\otimes_{\Perf(\Z_p)} \Perf(\Z/p^n)$.

Moreover, \cite[Proposition 15.4.1 and Equation (16.1.3)]{EmertonKisin2} give
\[\mathrm{RSol}_{\X}(\M)\mathord{/\mkern-6mu/} p^n \simeq \mathrm{RSol}_{\X,\Z/p^n}(\M \mathord{/\mkern-6mu/} p^n).\]
Thus the solution functor is naturally obtained by a compatible system of solution functors modulo $p^n$. Since for the mod $p$ reduction we have 
\[\@undefined^{b}_{\cons}(\X_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}, \F_p) \simeq \@undefined^{b}_{\cons}(\X_\ensuremath{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}},\F_p)\]
by \cite[Theorem 1.6(1)]{HemoRicharzScholbach2023}, \cite[Corollary 16.2.8]{EmertonKisin2} proves the equivalence by applying Lemma \ref{lem:categorical_nakayama}.

The perverse $t$-exactness claim remains. However, we gave reduction criteria in Definition \ref{def:EK_pplus}, so our strategy will be to reduce to checking it modulo $p$ where all the work is done in \cite{EmertonKisin2}.

Perverse $t$-exactness in \cite{EmertonKisin2} is actually proved for a variant with $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{F,\X}$-modules. This is not an issue, however. One notes that modulo $p$ \cite[Proposition 15.4.3]{EmertonKisin2} identifies the bounded derived category of finitely generated unit $\@undefined_{\mathrm{F},\mathscr{X}}$-modules with the usual finitely generated unit $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathrm{F},\X}$-modules, and \cite[16.1.5]{EmertonKisin2} identifies their solution functors. In particular we may work with $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathrm{F},\X}$-modules, even for perverse $t$-exactness, because the identification leaves the underlying $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathrm{F},\X}$-module unchanged (more precisely the identification is $t$-exact).

Assume now that $\X$ has pure dimension $d$, and consider $\mathrm{RSol}_{\X}(\M)[d]$. By derived Nakayama, $\M\in\@undefined^{\leq0}$ if and only if $\M\mathord{/\mkern-6mu/} p\in\@undefined^{\leq0}$. This compatibility with $-\mathord{/\mkern-6mu/} p$ and perverse $t$-exactness modulo $p$ from \cite[Theorem 11.5.4]{EmertonKisin2} (which applies to $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathrm{F},\X}$-modules) identifies the condition $\M\in\@undefined^{\leq0}$ with $(\mathrm{RSol}_{\X}(\M)[d])\mathord{/\mkern-6mu/} p\in{}^p\@undefined^{\geq0}$, which holds if and only if $\mathrm{RSol}_{\X}(\M)[d] \in {}^{p^+}\@undefined^{\geq0}$ by Definition \ref{def:EK_pplus}. Thus $\mathrm{RSol}$ identifies these halves of the two $t$-structures. Orthogonality identifies the other halves, and thus proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:EK_perfect}
Let $\R$ be a perfect $\F_p$-algebra. Then there is an equivalence
\[\mathrm{RSol}: \@undefined_{\fgu}(\W(\R))^\op \simeq \@undefined^{b}_{\mathrm{cons}}(\Spec \R, \Z_p)\]
given by $\underline{\mathrm{RHom}}_{\@undefined^{\varphi}(\W(\R)_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}})}(\M_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}, \W(\R)_\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}) \in \@undefined((\Spec \R)_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}},\Z_p)$. The equivalence is moreover symmetric monoidal.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
This is essentially already proven in \cite{BhattLurieModpRH}, but they work largely with $\F_p$ coefficients. The argument is similar to the previous case to make the extension to $\Z_p$ coefficients. Both sides are stable subcategories of their ambient derived categories closed under retracts, hence are idempotent complete and $\Perf(\Z_p)$-linear; the dual action of $\Perf(\Z_p)$ on the source makes $\mathrm{RSol}$ linear. Their reductions (in the sense of the setting of Lemma \ref{lem:categorical_nakayama}) are the perfect unit categories over $\W_n(\R)$ and the constructible complexes whose stalks have finite Tor-dimension over $\Z/p^n$.

Applying Lemma \ref{lem:categorical_nakayama} now reduces the claim to \cite[Theorem 11.4.4]{BhattLurieModpRH}, together with \cite[Theorems 12.5.4 and 12.6.1]{BhattLurieModpRH}.

Thus all the remains is to check the equivalence is symmetric monoidal. One may essentially copy the argument in \cite[Theorem 8.4.1]{BhattLurieModpRH}. The formula for $\mathrm{RSol}$ gives a lax symmetric monoidal structure:
\[\mathrm{RSol}(\M) \widehat{\otimes}_{\Z_p}^{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{RSol}(\mathrm{N}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{RSol}(\M \widehat{\otimes}_{\W(\R)}^{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{N}).\]
Both sides are derived $p$-complete, so derived Nakayama reduces the assertion that this map is an equivalence to the case modulo $p$, where it may be checked on geometric stalks (one must use pullback compatibility of the correspondence).

Over an algebraically closed perfect field $\kappa$, use the dual or contravariant form of Katz's theorem described in the remark following Theorem \ref{thm:katz}. The fact that this is symmetric monoidal can be checked in the same way as \cite[Theorem 8.4.1]{BhattLurieModpRH}: the category is equivalent to $\Perf(\F_p)$, and reducing to the heart (which is fine since it thickly generates) one can decompose objects as finite direct sums of the unit where the claim is obvious.

This argument hides that we needed to check another point, namely that we needed to check closure under tensor products. Remark \ref{rem:fgu_mod_p} reduces us to characteristic $p$, where \cite[Theorems 12.4.1 and 12.5.4, Proposition 12.3.8]{BhattLurieModpRH} express every finitely generated unit complex as $\@undefined(\mathrm{P})$ for a Frobenius complex $\mathrm{P}$ perfect over $\R$, where $\@undefined$ denotes a \textit{weak dual}. By \cite[Construction 11.2.7 and the proof of Proposition 12.5.1]{BhattLurieModpRH}, $\@undefined(\mathrm{P})\simeq\colim_n \varphi^{n*}(\mathrm{P}^\vee)$, so cofinality of the diagonal $\N\to\N^2$ allows us to deduce $\@undefined(\mathrm{P}) \otimes_{\R}^{\mathrm{L}} \@undefined(\mathrm{Q}) \simeq \@undefined(\mathrm{P}\otimes_{\R}^{\mathrm{L}}\mathrm{Q})$ by indexing the colimit over the diagonal. Since $\mathrm{P} \otimes_{\R}^{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{Q}$ is again perfect over $\R$, its weak dual is finitely generated unit by \cite[Proposition 12.3.11]{BhattLurieModpRH}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
Let $\X/\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K$ be smooth and quasicompact, let $\@undefined$ be a horizontal normal crossings divisor\footnote{By this we mean that $\@undefined\cup\X_s$ is a normal crossings divisor and no irreducible component of $\@undefined$ is contained in the special fiber; equivalently, strict \'{e}tale locally the pair has the form of Definition \ref{def:fr_log_aff}}, and let $\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}_\@undefined$ be the log structure induced by $\@undefined$.
\label{ass:snc_log_structure}
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $K$ be a complete nonarchimedean field of mixed characteristic $(0,p)$. A framing of $(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})$ over $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K$ is a $p$-completely \'{e}tale map $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K\langle \T_1,\ldots,\T_r,\T_{r+1}^{\pm},\ldots,\T_n^{\pm}\rangle\to\R$ under which $\mathcal{M}$ is the pullback of the log structure with chart $\N^r$ whose generators map to $\T_1,\ldots,\T_r$. We denote the resulting log formal scheme $\Spf \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K\langle \T_1,\ldots,\T_r,\T_{r+1}^{\pm},\ldots,\T_n^{\pm}\rangle$ by $\mathbb{T}_r^n$, the framing map by $\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}$, and call $(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})$ a \textit{framed log affine}.
\label{def:fr_log_aff}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:fr_log_aff_W(k)_model}
For a framed log affine, we use $n$ and $r$ as the corresponding integers in Definition \ref{def:fr_log_aff}. We sometimes call the \'{e}tale lifts of $\T_1,\ldots,\T_r$ ``boundary coordinates''.

If $K/\W(k)[1/p]$ is finite with residue field $k$, the framing descends to $\W(k)$. There is a $p$-completely \'{e}tale $\W(k)\langle \T_1,\ldots,\T_r,\T_{r+1}^{\pm},\ldots,\T_n^{\pm}\rangle$-algebra $\R_0$ with $\R\simeq\R_0\widehat\otimes_{\W(k)}\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K$, compatibly with the framing. Indeed, for a uniformizer $\pi$ of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K$, lift the \'{e}tale algebra $\R/\pi$ to $\R_0$ over the corresponding $\W(k)$-algebra.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
Let $(\X,\mathcal{M})$ satisfy Assumption \ref{ass:snc_log_structure} over $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K$. Then $(\X,\mathcal{M})$ admits a finite strict \'{e}tale cover by framed log affines over $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K$.
\label{lem:strict_etale_local_framing}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
This is surely well-known, but we include a proof for completeness. We first observe that our normal crossings setting, working strict \'{e}tale locally immediately allows us to separate the local branches of $\@undefined$ and reduce to the situation where $\@undefined$ is a simple normal crossings divisor.

Once we are in this situation, let us zoom in around a closed point $x\in \X$ (which we equip with its pullback log structure) and denote the irreducible components of $\@undefined$ passing through $x$ by $\@undefined_1, \ldots, \@undefined_r$. We can pick a small affine Zariski neighborhood $\Spf \R$ of $x$, so no other components besides these $\@undefined_i$ meet this neighborhood.

In this situation we must now produce a framing for $\Spf \R$. Since $\@undefined$ is a simple normal crossings divisor after possibly shrinking further there are elements $t_1,\ldots,t_r,s_{r+1},\ldots,s_n\in\R$ such that $\@undefined_i=\V(t_i)$ and
\[\mathrm{d}t_1,\ldots,\mathrm{d}t_r,\mathrm{d}s_{r+1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}s_n\]
is a basis of $\widehat{\Omega}^1_{\R/\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K}$. Choose constants $c_j\in\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_K$ such that $u_j=s_j+c_j$ has nonzero image in $\kappa(x)$; thus after Zariski localizing further, each $u_j$ is a unit. We can even choose $c_j$ so they are zero or one. Using the functions $t_i$ and $u_j$ for the images of the coordinates in $\mathbb{T}_r^n$ they define a morphism
\[\Spf \R \xlongrightarrow{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}} \mathbb{T}_r^n.\]
That is, it is induced by the ring map sending $\T_i$ to $t_i$ for $i\leq r$ and $\T_j$ to $u_j$ for $j>r$ (the latter are invertible, which is why we localized to make $u_j$ units).

The pullback of $\V(\T_1\cdots\T_r)$ is $\V(t_1\cdots t_r)=\@undefined\cap\Spf\R$, hence $\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}$ is strict as a morphism of log formal schemes. Since on stalks by construction the pullback induced by $\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}$ on $\Omega^1$ is an isomorphism this shows that the underlying morphism is $p$-completely \'{e}tale.

Quasicompactness gives a finite cover.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
Let $(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})$ be a framed log affine and put $\overline{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{A}/p$. Let $\M$ be a finite $\overline{\mathrm{A}}$-module equipped with a continuous semilinear $\Gamma$-action as above. Suppose there is a $\Gamma$-equivariant injection 
\[\M\hookrightarrow\varphi^*\M.\] 
Then there is a coherent Laurent crystal $\mathcal{E}$ killed by $p$, with $\rho_{\mathrm{A}}^\ast(\mathcal{E})=\M$, and an injection $\mathcal{E}\hookrightarrow\varphi^*\mathcal{E}$ whose evaluation is the given map.
\label{thm:laur_root_crys}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
Let $\mathrm{A}^+=\R_0^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\llbracket q-1\rrbracket$, and let $(\mathrm{A}^+)^{(1)}$ be the ring of the self-coproduct of $(\mathrm{A}^+,[p]_q,\mathcal{M})^a$ in the category of log prisms $(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}^{\mathrm{op}}$. Write $q_0,q_1$ for the two copies of $q$, put $u_0=q_1/q_0$, and let $u_i=\T_{i,1}/\T_{i,0}$ for $1\leq i\leq n$. Then
\[(\mathrm{A}^+)^{(1)} \simeq \R_0^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\llbracket q_0-1\rrbracket[u_0^{\pm1},u_1^{\pm1},\ldots,u_n^{\pm1}]\left\{\frac{u_0-1}{[p]_{q_0}},\ldots,\frac{u_n-1}{[p]_{q_0}}\right\}_{\delta,(p,[p]_{q_0})}^{\wedge}.\]
Here $\delta(u_j)=0$ for $0\leq j\leq n$.
\label{lem:qdr_actual_cech_envelope}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
This can be checked directly by matching the universal properties of the prismatic envelope. We omit this here, since we prove a more general claim in Lemma \ref{lem:prism_coproduct}. There we handle the general Breuil-Kisin case. The $\delta$-structure used in that argument is different, but the argument is identical.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
We use slightly different coordinates for $\Gamma$, where the coordinate $x_0$ for $a\in 1+p\Z_p$ records $x_0=\frac{a-1}{p}$ and for $b_i \in \Z_p(1)\simeq \Z_p$ we use the coordinate $x_i$ for $1\leq i\leq n$. Thus we obtain a system of coordinates $x=(x_0,\ldots, x_n)$ for $\Gamma$.

Set $\eta_{0,m}(x_0)=q^{m+p\binom{m}{2}}(q-1)^m\binom{x_0}{m}_{q^p}$ and $\eta_{i,m}(x_i)=q^{p\binom{m}{2}}(q-1)^m\binom{x_i}{m}_{q^p}$ for $i>0$. Write $\eta_\alpha$ for the products of these functions in the $(n+1)$ variables and set
\[\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}) = \left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\N^{n+1}}\mathrm{A}^+\eta_\alpha\right)^{\wedge}_{(p,q-1)}[1/[p]_q]^{\wedge}_p.\]
We define $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{A})$ similarly, over indices $\alpha\in \N^{s(n+1)}$.\footnote{There is also an alternative formula which will be of use. Consider the divided powers
\[[m]_{q^p}!\gamma_{m,q^p}(x)=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}((q^p)^x-q^{pj}),\]
where $[m]_{q^p}!=\prod_{j=1}^m[j]_{q^p}$. Then $\eta_{0,m}(x_0)=q^m[p]_q^{-m}\gamma_{m,q^p}(x_0)$ and $\eta_{i,m}(x_i)=[p]_q^{-m}\gamma_{m,q^p}(x_i)$ for $i>0$.}
\label{def:Cq}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
The map $\theta_s$ identifies $\mathrm{A}^{(s)}$ with the subring $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{A})\subset\mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{A})$:
\[\mathrm{A}^{(s)}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{A}).\]
This is further an isomorphism $\AnSpf \mathrm{A}^{(s)} \simeq \AnSpf \mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{A})$.
\label{lem:Cech_function_calc}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
As above, we use $\mathrm{A}=\R_0^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\mathopen{(\mkern-3mu(}q-1\mathclose{)\mkern-3mu)}_p^{\wedge}$. We first treat $s=1$. We actually will show a stronger claim, which is that there is a natural isomorphism of adic rings
\[\theta_1: \mathrm{A}^{+,(1)}\simeq \left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\N^{n+1}}\mathrm{A}^+\eta_\alpha\right)^{\wedge}_{(p,q-1)}.\]
After $p$-completely inverting $[p]_q$ or equivalently $q-1$, this isomorphism of ordinary adic rings implies the desired isomorphism of analytic stacks.

We do this by using the explicit log prismatic envelope presentation of $\mathrm{A}^{+,(1)}$. Recall $(\mathrm{A}^+)^{(1)}$ from Lemma \ref{lem:qdr_actual_cech_envelope} is the $(p,q-1)$-adic (equivalently $(p,[p]_q)$) completion of
\[\mathrm{A}^+[u_0^{\pm1},\ldots,u_n^{\pm1}]\left\{\frac{u_0-1}{[p]_{q_0}},\ldots,\frac{u_n-1}{[p]_{q_0}}\right\}_{\delta}.\]
We used $u_0=q_1/q_0$ and $u_i=\T_{i,1}/\T_{i,0}$ as shorthand. The map $\theta_1$ can be made explicit integrally. For $g\in\Gamma$, using the coordinates $g=(x_0,\ldots, x_n)$ of Definition \ref{def:Cq}, the evaluation of $\theta_1(a) \in \Map(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^+)$\footnote{We haven't yet checked the output is a continuous function.} for $a\in \mathrm{A}^{+,(1)}$ at $g$ is obtained by applying the $\mathrm{A}^+$-algebra map determined by $u_i\mapsto(q^p)^{x_i(g)}$ for $0\leq i\leq n$.

Using \cite[Theorem 4.4]{GrosLeStumQuiros2023}, $\mathrm{A}^+[u_0^{\pm1}]\left\{\frac{u_0-1}{[p]_{q_0}}\right\}^{\wedge}_{\delta}$ is, up to a change of variables, the $(p,q-1)$-completion of the free $\mathrm{A}^+$-module on their ${\mathbbl{\Delta}}$-divided powers $\omega_{0,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{\{n\}}$ (see \cite[Definition 1.7]{GrosLeStumQuiros2023}) as a $(p,q-1)$-adic ring. Indeed from the discussion preceding Theorem 4.4 in \cite{GrosLeStumQuiros2023} they identify $\widehat{\bigoplus}_{n\ge 0} \mathrm{A}^+ \omega_{0,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{\{n\}}$ with the prismatic envelope of the $\delta$-pair $(\mathrm{A}^+ \llbracket \xi \rrbracket,(\xi))$, which checking universal properties is indeed our ring (one has $\xi \mapsto q_0(u_0-1)$).

Now we see where $\theta_1$ sends this basis. Using \cite[Remark 1.8(5)]{GrosLeStumQuiros2023} provides a ``blowing up'' map $\mathrm{Bl}$, yielding
\[\mathrm{A}^+ \langle \xi \rangle_{q_0^p} \xlongrightarrow{\mathrm{Bl}} \widehat{\bigoplus}_{n\ge 0} \mathrm{A}^+ \omega_{0,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{\{n\}} \simeq \mathrm{A}^+[u_0^{\pm1}]\left\{\frac{u_0-1}{[p]_{q_0}}\right\}^{\wedge}_{\delta} \xlongrightarrow{\theta_1} \Map(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^+)\]
such that the $q$-divided power $\xi^{[m]_{q_0^p}}$ is sent to $[p]_{q_0}^m \omega_{0,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}^{\{m\}}$ under $\mathrm{Bl}$. This is helpful, because we know where $\xi^{[m]_{q_0^p}}$ is sent to under the composite map $\theta_1 \circ \mathrm{Bl}$: $\xi$ is sent by $\theta_1$ to
\[q((q^{p})^{x_0}-1) \in \Map(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^+).\]
Thus we may deduce
\[[p]_{q_0}^m \theta_1(\omega^{\{m\}}_{0,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}) = q^m\gamma_{m,q^p}(x_0),\]
so in particular using the alternative formula in the footnote for Definition \ref{def:Cq} we see $\theta_1(\omega^{\{m\}}_{0,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}})=\eta_{0,m}$ using $[p]_{q_0}$-torsionfreeness. 

Next, we handle the remaining factors corresponding to $u_i$ for $i>0$. The argument is more or less the same. Using \cite[Definition 1.6 and Corollary 5.6]{GrosLeStumQuirosNegative}, the corresponding factor $\mathrm{A}^+[u_i^{\pm1}]\left\{\frac{u_i-1}{[p]_{q_0}}\right\}^{\wedge}_{\delta}$ is the completion of the free $\mathrm{A}^+$-module on divided powers $\omega^{\{m\}}_{i,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}$, in their notation. The analogous map in \cite[Proposition 1.7]{GrosLeStumQuirosNegative} lets us deduce the formula
\[[p]_q^m\theta_1(\omega^{\{m\}}_{i,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}})=\gamma_{m,q^p}(x_i).\]
Similarly we find $\theta_1(\omega^{\{m\}}_{i,{\mathbbl{\Delta}}}) = \eta_{i,m}$. Thus $\theta_1$ induces a surjection onto
\[\left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\N^{n+1}}\mathrm{A}^+\eta_\alpha\right)^{\wedge}_{(p,q-1)}.\]
It is injective: evaluation at nonnegative integral values of each $x_i$ is triangular, with $\eta_{i,m}(j)=0$ for $m>j$ and $\eta_{i,m}(m)$ a unit times $(q-1)^m$. Only finitely many terms contribute at each such value, and $\mathrm{A}^+$ is $(q-1)$-torsion-free. Hence the integral map is, as desired, an isomorphism onto $\left(\bigoplus_\alpha\mathrm{A}^+\eta_\alpha\right)^{\wedge}_{(p,q-1)}$; the isomorphism is of $(p,q-1)$-adic rings, so the desired claim about analytic stacks also follows. One sees $\theta_1$ lands in $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ by the discussion after Definition \ref{def:Cq}.

For general $s$, $\mathrm{A}^{+,(s)}=(\mathrm{A}^{+(1)})^{\widehat{\otimes}^s_{\mathrm{A}^+}}$. Using this one may check
\[(\mathrm{A}^+)^{(s)}\simeq\left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\N^{s(n+1)}}\mathrm{A}^+\eta_\alpha\right)^{\wedge}_{(p,q-1)},\]
so by the same argument the general claim follows.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
Let $\B$ and $\mathrm{G}$ be as above. Give $\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G}^s,\B)$ its natural analytic ring structure, and assume $\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G}^s,\B)$ is $p$-completely nuclear over $\B$. Then the functor
\[\lim_{[s]\in\Delta}\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G}^s,\B)) \longrightarrow \Rep_{\B_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}^{t}}(\mathrm{G})\]
restricts to an equivalence from objects whose evaluation at $[0]$ is $p$-completely nuclear\footnote{By this we mean it is derived $p$-complete and satisfies the nuclearity property for derived $p$-complete objects; equivalently, it is derived $p$-complete and nuclear mod $p$.} to representations whose underlying $\B$-module is $p$-completely nuclear. 

If $\M\in \@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B)$ is the underlying solid $\B$-module under this equivalence,
\[\varprojlim_{[s]\in\Delta}\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G}^s,\B) \otimes_{\B}^{\mathrm{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}} \M \simeq \varprojlim_{[s]\in\Delta}\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G}^s,\M) \simeq \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\mathrm{G},\M).\]
\label{lem:nuclear_continuous_action}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
We use a similar argument to \cite[Corollary 1.50]{MikamiRelativelyDiscrete}. The Barr-Beck-Lurie theorem identifies the source and target with coalgebras in $\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B)$ for the following comonads. The first is induced by the endofunctor
\[\mathbb{T}:\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B) \xrightarrow{ \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\B)\otimes_{\B}^{\mathrm{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}- } \@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\B)) \longrightarrow \@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B).\]
Here the first morphism uses the map $\B \to \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\B)$ sending $b\in \B$ to the constant function (valued at $b$). The second morphism is pushforward along the action map $\mathrm{act}: \B \to \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\B)$ (i.e. $b$ is sent to the function sending $g$ to $g(b)$). The comonad structure is the obvious one (the comultiplication is induced by the multiplication on $\mathrm{G}$).

The second comonad is induced by the endofunctor $\mathbb{S}:\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B)\to\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B)$ given by
\[\mathbb{S}(\M)=\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\M),\]
where $(b f)(g)=g(b)f(g)$ on $\mathbb S(\M)$. Thus
\[\varprojlim_{[s]\in\Delta}\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G}^s,\B)) \simeq \mathrm{CoAlg}_{\mathbb T}(\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B)).\]
Similarly, $\Rep_{\B_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}^{t}}(\mathrm{G}) \simeq \mathrm{CoAlg}_{\mathbb S}(\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B))$. 

The map $f\otimes m \mapsto (g\mapsto f(g)m)$ defines a natural transformation $\mathbb{T} \to \mathbb{S}$ compatible with the counits and comultiplications, hence a map of comonads.

Suppose now that $\M$ is $p$-completely nuclear. For the compact object $\mathrm{P}=\B[\underline{\mathrm{G}}]$, nuclearity and the identifications $\mathrm{P}^\vee\simeq\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\B)$ and $\underline{\mathrm{RHom}}_{\B}(\mathrm{P},\M)\simeq\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\M)$ give
\[\mathbb{T}(\M) = \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\B)\otimes_{\B}^{\mathrm{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\M \simeq \mathrm{P}^\vee\otimes_{\B}^{\mathrm{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\M \simeq \underline{\mathrm{RHom}}_{\B}(\mathrm{P},\M) \simeq \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\M) = \mathbb{S}(\M).\]
By the assumed $p$-complete nuclearity of $\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{G},\B)$ and closure of nuclear objects under tensor products, both comonads restrict to the full subcategory of $p$-completely nuclear modules in $\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B)$. The preceding calculation then identifies their restrictions as comonads, so coalgebra categories are therefore equivalent which proves the claim.

The cohomological comparison follows by taking $\RHom$ with the unit.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
Let $\bar{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{A}/p$ (similarly for $\bar{\mathrm{A}}^+$) and consider $f\in \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\bar{\mathrm{A}})$. We take its Mahler expansion
\[f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in \N^{n+1}} a_\alpha\binom{x}{\alpha},\]
where $\binom{x}{\alpha}=\prod_i\binom{x_i}{\alpha_i}$. Suppose there are constants $\sigma>1$ and $\mathrm{C}$ for which
\[a_\alpha\in(q-1)^{\lceil\sigma|\alpha|-\mathrm{C}\rceil}\bar{\mathrm{A}}^+\]
for every multi-index $\alpha$. Then $f\in\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})$.
\label{lem:Cq_criterion}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We will prove the stronger assertion
\[\left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in \N^{n+1}}\overline{\mathrm{A}}^+\eta_\alpha\right)^\wedge_{(q-1)} = \left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in \N^{n+1}}\overline{\mathrm{A}}^+ (q-1)^{|\alpha|}\binom{x}{\alpha}\right)^\wedge_{(q-1)}.\]

We first compute the Mahler expansions of the $\eta_{\alpha}$ from Definition \ref{def:Cq}. As discussed above, to compute the coefficients if $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ we must work out the coefficients
\[(\Delta_0^{\beta_0} \cdots \Delta_n^{\beta_n}\eta_{\alpha})(0)\]
of the expansion of $\eta_\alpha$ into binomial coefficients.

Recall that for $i>0$ we have $\eta_{i,m}(x_i)=(q-1)^m \cdot q^{p\binom{m}{2}}\binom{x_i}{m}_{q^p}$. Because we work in $\mathrm{A}=\R_0^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\mathopen{(\mkern-3mu(}q-1\mathclose{)\mkern-3mu)}_p^{\wedge}$ the leading factor can be ignored. The Mahler expansion of a $q$-binomial coefficient can be computed using the recurrence
\[\Delta_i \binom{x_i}{m}_{q^p} = \binom{x_i+1}{m}_{q^p} - \binom{x_i}{m}_{q^p} = (q^{pm}-1)\binom{x_i}{m}_{q^p} + \binom{x_i}{m-1}_{q^p}.\]
Bringing back the scaling factors $(q-1)^m \cdot q^{p\binom{m}{2}}$, this yields $\Delta_i \eta_{i,m} = (q^{pm}-1)\eta_{i,m} + (q-1)q^{p(m-1)}\eta_{i,m-1}$. For $i=0$ the result is similar, since these differ only by a factor of $q^m$ (which is irrelevant in the argument that follows).

This immediately tells us some of the Mahler coefficients. Namely, it tells us that the coefficient of $\binom{x_i}{j}$ for $\eta_{i,m}$ vanishes for $j<m$ and is $(q-1)^m \cdot \mathrm{unit}$ for $j=m$. The first claim is simply because $\eta_{i,m}(j)=0$ when $j<m$. For the second, note from the previous recurrence
\[\Delta^m_i \eta_{i,m}(0) = (q-1)q^{p(m-1)} \Delta^{m-1}_i \eta_{i,m-1}(0)\]
so thus upon iterating this we get $(q-1)^m \cdot \mathrm{unit}$ as the coefficient of $\binom{x_i}{m}$. For higher terms, all that matters is that a similar argument shows when $j>m$ the coefficient of $\binom{x_i}{j}$ in $\eta_{i,m}$ is in $(q-1)^{m+p(j-m)} \cdot (\R_0^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\llbracket q-1 \rrbracket/p)$. 

In summary, we have shown that in $\overline{\mathrm{A}}^+ = (\R_0^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\llbracket q-1 \rrbracket/p)$ we have
\[\eta_{i,m}=u_{i,m}(q-1)^m\binom{x_i}{m}+\sum_{j>m}c_{i,m,j} (q-1)^j \binom{x_i}{j}.\]
Here $u_{i,m}\in(\overline{\mathrm{A}}^+)^\times$, and $c_{i,m,j}\in(q-1)^{(p-1)(j-m)}\overline{\mathrm{A}}^+$, relating the two proposed bases of $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})$. Since this is an upper triangular change of basis where the off diagonal part is a topologically nilpotent operator, the claim follows. More precisely this shows the $(q-1)^{|\alpha|}\binom{x}{\alpha}$ and the $\eta_\alpha$ bases are related by an operator $\@undefined(1+\mathrm{N})$ where $\@undefined$ is diagonal and invertible and
\[\mathrm{N}^r \left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in \N^{n+1}}\overline{\mathrm{A}}^+ (q-1)^{|\alpha|}\binom{x}{\alpha}\right)^\wedge_{(q-1)} \subset (q-1)^{(p-1)r} \left(\bigoplus_{\alpha \in \N^{n+1}} \overline{\mathrm{A}}^+ (q-1)^{|\alpha|}\binom{x}{\alpha}\right)^\wedge_{(q-1)},\]
hence $\mathrm{N}$ is topologically nilpotent. Thus we deduce the claimed isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Interestingly this shows that modulo $p$ we have $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}}) = \mathrm{C}_{\lambda-\mathrm{an}}(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})$ where $\lambda = - \log_p(p-1)$ as in \cite{PoratSolidLocallyAnalytic}. Strictly speaking Porat does not allow $\lambda < 0$, but as noted in \cite[Definition 4.1, footnote 1]{HauckLA} the definition still makes sense.
\label{rem:la_Cq}
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
Right translation defines a continuous $\Gamma$-action on $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ by $(\gamma f)(g)=f(g\gamma)$. Then there is a natural equivalence
\begin{display}
\mathrm{A} \ar{r}{\sim} & \mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\bigl(\Gamma,\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})).
\end{display}
\label{lem:Cech_cohomology}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By derived Nakayama it is enough to work modulo $p$. The proof of Lemma \ref{lem:Cq_criterion} shows there is a lattice
\[\left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\N^{n+1}} \overline{\mathrm{A}}^+(q-1)^{|\alpha|}\binom{x}{\alpha}\right)^{\wedge}_{q-1} \subset \mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})\]
Let $\Fil^\bullet$ be the $q-1$-adic filtration on this lattice; this filtration is complete and separated.

Let $\gamma_0,\ldots, \gamma_n$ be the usual generators of $\Gamma$, in the coordinates $x_i$ of $\Gamma$ chosen in Lemma \ref{lem:Cq_criterion}. Writing down the action $(\gamma f)(g) := f(g\gamma)$ on $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ explicitly, we see right multiplication by $\gamma_i$ acts on $g=(x_0,\ldots,x_n)$ by sending $x_i \mapsto x_i + 1 + px_0$.

The desired claim will follow by showing that modulo $p$ the complex
\[\left[\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}}) \xrightarrow{\gamma_i-\id} \mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})\right]\]
is naturally quasi-isomorphic to the functions in $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})$ which are independent of $x_i$ (placed in degree zero). Thus if we iterate this, using (\ref{eq:solid_group_resolution}) shows that we get $\overline{\mathrm{A}}$ as $\mathrm{R}\Gamma_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\bigl(\Gamma,\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}))$; one uses Hochschild-Serre to work with $\Gamma$ rather than $\Z_p^n$, by dealing with $\Z_p^n$ first and then $1+p\Z_p$. Let us denote by $\pi_i: \mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}) \to \mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ the projection onto functions independent of $x_i$.

This can be done explicitly. The idea is to argue that $\gamma_i-\id$ is a perturbation of the finite difference operator $\Delta_i$ which acts on $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ (for the coordinate $x_i$). Here we use that $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ is a ring and stable under the coordinate change $x_i \mapsto x_{i}+1$. For $\Delta_i$ the claim is clear, because in
\[\left[\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})\xrightarrow{\Delta_i}\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})\right]\]
the kernel consists of functions independent of $x_i$, and it is surjective since we can define
\[h_i\left((q-1)^{|\alpha|}\binom{x}{\alpha}\right)=(q-1)^{|\alpha|}\binom{x_i}{\alpha_i+1}\prod_{j\ne i}\binom{x_j}{\alpha_j}\]
giving a continuous endomorphism of $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}})$ such that $\Delta_i h_i=\id$. 

Now we observe that 
\[(\gamma_i-\id) \cdot f(x_0,\ldots,x_n) = f(x_0,\ldots,x_i + 1 + px_0, \ldots, x_n) - f(x_0,\ldots,x_n).\]
In particular, $\gamma_i-\id$ is nearly the finite difference operator $\Delta_i$ except for the $px_0$ term. We have a commutative diagram
\begin{display}
\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}}) \ar{r}{\gamma_i-\id} & \mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}}) \\
\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}}) \ar{u}{\id} \ar{r}{\Delta_i} & \mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}}) \ar{u}{(\gamma_i-\id)h_i}.
\end{display}
We claim $(\gamma_i-\id)h_i$ differs from $\id$ by an operator that carries $\Fil^r$ into $\Fil^{r+p-2}$. Indeed note that 
\[(\gamma_i-\id)h_i - \id = ((\gamma_i-\id)-\Delta_i)h_i.\]
Following the effect of $(\gamma_i-\id)-\Delta_i$ on $\binom{x_i}{\alpha}$, we note the identity 
\[((\gamma_i-\id)-\Delta_i) \cdot \binom{x_i}{\alpha} = \binom{(x_i+1)+px_0}{\alpha}- \binom{x_i+1}{\alpha} = \sum_{\ell \ge 1} \binom{x_i+1}{\alpha-p\ell} \binom{x_0}{\ell}\]
modulo $p$. In particular, using this for $(q-1)^{|\alpha|}\binom{x}{\alpha}$ shows $(\gamma_i-\id)-\Delta_i$ sends $\Fil^r$ into $\Fil^{r+p-1}$ (for the $q-1$-adic filtration). Inspecting the formula for $h_i$, we then deduce $((\gamma_i-\id)-\Delta_i)h_i$ sends $\Fil^r$ into $\Fil^{r+p-2}$. As $p>2$, this is filtration raising and $(\gamma_i-\id)h_i$ has an inverse.

We conclude in the previous diagram that there is a quasi-isomorphism between the rows, so the desired claim follows.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
Evaluation on the log $q$-de Rham prism attached to $\mathrm{A}^+=\R_0^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\square$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\square$}}}}\llbracket q-1\rrbracket$ induces a fully faithful functor
\[\rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,*}: \@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}((\Spf\R,\mathcal{M})_{\mathbbl{\Delta}},\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}[1/\I_{\mathbbl{\Delta}}]_p^{\wedge}) \longrightarrow \@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\mathrm{A})^{h\Gamma}.\]
When the evaluation on the log $q$-de Rham prism is $p$-completely nuclear, the target can be thought of as semilinear $\Gamma$-modules by the equivalence of Lemma \ref{lem:nuclear_continuous_action}.
\label{prop:Gamma_mod_ff}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Under the stack/site equivalence of Proposition \ref{prop:stack_site_compare}, $\rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,*}$ is induced on $\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(-)$ by pullback along
\[\rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A}}: [\AnSpf \mathrm{A}/\Gamma] \longrightarrow (\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}.\]
See Definition \ref{def:anspf} for the meaning of $\AnSpf$. Taking the presentation $\colim_{[n]\in \Delta^\op} \AnSpf \mathrm{A}^{(n)}$ of the target given by Proposition \ref{prop:log_BK_analytic_presentation} after base change to $(\X,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}$ and the natural presentation $\colim_{[n]\in \Delta^\op} \AnSpf \mathrm{C}(\Gamma^n,\mathrm{A})$ of the source one obtains the description of the functor appearing before Lemma \ref{lem:Cech_function_calc}. Here, both presentations are obtained by taking the \v{C}ech nerve of the cover by $\AnSpf \mathrm{A}$. We note that one should not construct this map by claiming only that the map $\AnSpf \mathrm{A} \to (\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}$ obtained from the fpqc epimorphism of formal stacks obtained in Lemma \ref{lem:log_prism_stack_map} is $\Gamma$-equivariant, because a priori the action might not be continuous. But once one uses presentations of both stacks and Lemma \ref{lem:Cech_function_calc} to check the action is continuous, as in the site-theoretic construction it becomes well-defined.

The assertion reduces to cohomological properness of $\rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A}}$ in the sense of \cite[Definition 2.1.3.1]{Kipp}, which we prove in Lemma \ref{lem:rho_cohom_prop}. We use the same conventions as \cite{Kipp}, and work with the six functor formalism on analytic stacks. In our case the analytic stacks all lie over $\AnSpec \Z_{p,\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}$ with its solid analytic ring structure.

The claim that $\rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,\ast}$ is fully faithful amounts to the claim that the map
\[\RHom(\mathcal{E}',\mathcal{E}) \longrightarrow \RHom(\rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,\ast} \mathcal{E}', \rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,\ast} \mathcal{E}) \simeq \RHom(\mathcal{E}', \R \rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A},*} \rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,\ast} \mathcal{E})\]
is an isomorphism. It therefore is equivalent to check $\R \rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A},*} \rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,\ast} \mathcal{E} \simeq \mathcal{E}$. As $\rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A}}$ is cohomologically proper, we have access to the projection formula and can compute
\[\R \rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A},*} \rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,\ast} \mathcal{E} \simeq \R \rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A},!}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}} \otimes^{\mathrm{L}} \rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma,\ast} \mathcal{E}) \simeq \R \rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A},\ast} \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}} \otimes^{\mathrm{L}} \mathcal{E}.\]
In particular we must show the canonical map $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}} \to \R \rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A},\ast} \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}/\Gamma]}$ is an isomorphism.

This task can be simplified further. Again as $\rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A}}$ is cohomologically proper we also have proper base change. We will use the square
\begin{display}
{[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}^{(1)}/\Gamma]} \ar{d}{f} \ar{r} & {[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}/\Gamma]} \ar{d}{\rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A}}} \\
\AnSpf \mathrm{A} \ar{r}{\rho_{\mathrm{A}}} & (\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}.
\end{display}
This square is Cartesian, using that $\AnSpf \mathrm{A} \times_{(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}} \AnSpf \mathrm{A} = \AnSpf \mathrm{A}^{(1)}$ from the \v{C}ech nerve presentation of $(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}$ in Proposition \ref{prop:log_BK_analytic_presentation}. Note that the $\Gamma$ action is nontrivial in $[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}^{(1)}/\Gamma]$ as it is acting by right translation. For the unit $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}} \in \@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}([\AnSpf \mathrm{A}/\Gamma])$ properness gives a base change isomorphism
\begin{display}
\rho_{\mathrm{A}}^* \R\rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A},*} \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}} \ar{r}{\sim} & \R f_* \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}.
\end{display}
Formally, showing $\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{(\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}} \to \R \rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A},\ast} \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}_{[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}/\Gamma]}$ is an isomorphism then reduces to the cohomology computation that the canonical map $\mathrm{A} \to \R\Gamma_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\Gamma, \mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}))$ is an equivalence. It is here that we use that the unit is $p$-completely nuclear, so $\R f_* \ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}$ can be computed as solid group cohomology. This calculation was done in Lemma \ref{lem:Cech_cohomology}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:rho_cohom_prop}
The map 
\[\rho_{\mathrm{A}}^{\Gamma}: [\AnSpf \mathrm{A}/\Gamma] \longrightarrow (\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\]
constructed in Proposition \ref{prop:Gamma_mod_ff} is cohomologically proper.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Proposition \ref{prop:log_BK_analytic_presentation} and base change to the Laurent stack $(\X,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}$ show that $\rho_{\mathrm{A}}: \AnSpf \mathrm{A} \to (\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}$ is a representable proper effective epimorphism. Thus we only need to deal with the quotient by $\Gamma$.

Since properness is local on the target for such covers by \cite[Remark 1.1.3.7]{Kipp}, it suffices to check the claim for
\[[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}^{(1)}/\Gamma] \longrightarrow \AnSpf \mathrm{A}\]
where we again use the square
\begin{display}
{[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}^{(1)}/\Gamma]} \ar{d}{f} \ar{r} & {[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}/\Gamma]} \ar{d}{\rho^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{A}}} \\
\AnSpf \mathrm{A} \ar{r}{\rho_{\mathrm{A}}} & (\Spf \R,\mathcal{M})^{\mathcal{L},\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}.
\end{display}
This property is stable under base change, so this can be also checked using $\mathrm{A}^+$ and $\mathrm{A}^{+,(1)}$. The right translation action involved in $[\AnSpf \mathrm{A}^{(1)}/\Gamma]$ fixes the image of $\mathrm{A}^+$, giving a factorization of the map as
\[[\AnSpec \mathrm{A}^{+,(1)}/\Gamma]\longrightarrow \AnSpec \mathrm{A}^+\times \B\Gamma\longrightarrow \AnSpec \mathrm{A}^+.\]
Note we are using $(p,[p]_q)$-adic rings now, so we also use the notation $\Spa(\mathrm{A}^{+,(1)},\mathrm{A}^{+,(1)})$ elsewhere for $\AnSpec \mathrm{A}^{+,(1)}$ as used here. After base change, pulling the first map back along $\AnSpec \mathrm{A}^+ \to \AnSpec \mathrm{A}^+\times B\Gamma$ gives $\AnSpec \mathrm{A}^{+,(1)}\to\AnSpec \mathrm{A}^+$, which is proper by Lemma \ref{lem:prismatic_product_adic_descendable}. It remains to show that
\[\B \Gamma \longrightarrow \AnSpec \Z_{p,\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\]
is proper for the six functor formalism on analytic stacks. One may use an argument similar to \cite[Proposition 5.3.2]{HeyerMannSixFunctors}. The map $g:\AnSpec \Z_{p,\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\to\B\Gamma$ is representable and proper, while $\B \Gamma \to \AnSpec \Z_{p,\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}$ is $1$-truncated and its composite with $g$ is the identity. By \cite[Corollary 4.7.5(iii)]{HeyerMannSixFunctors}, it remains only to verify that $g_*\ensuremath{\mathcal{O}}=\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\Z_p)$ is descendable. The resolution in (\ref{eq:solid_group_resolution}), applied to the normal subgroup $\Z_p(1)^n$ and quotient $1+p\Z_p\simeq\Z_p$, shows that the trivial representation $\Z_p$ is perfect over $\Z_p\llbracket\Gamma\rrbracket$. Taking derived solid $\Z_p$-duals and using $\Z_p\llbracket\Gamma\rrbracket^\vee\simeq\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\Z_p)$ gives
\[\Z_p\in\mathrm{Thick}\bigl(\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\Z_p)\bigr)\subset\@undefined_{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\B\Gamma),\]
as desired.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
Let $\mathrm{A}$ be a topological ring, and let $\Gamma$ be a profinite group acting continuously on $\mathrm{A}$. We make two topological assumptions on $\mathrm{A}$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item The topology on $\mathrm{A}$ is complete Hausdorff metrizable.
  \item The ring $\mathrm{A}$ has the property that a finitely generated module $\M\subseteq \mathrm{A}^n$ has its weak topology agree with its subspace topology.
\end{itemize} 
Let $\Mod^{\mathrm{fp}}(\mathrm{A})$ be the category of finitely presented $\mathrm{A}$-modules. Then there is an equivalence
\[F: \Mod^{\mathrm{fp}}(\mathrm{A})^{h\Gamma}\simeq \left\{\begin{gathered}\M\in \Mod^{\mathrm{fp}}_{\mathrm{A}} \text{ with } \Gamma\times\M\to\M \\ \text{ continuous for the weak topology on } \M\end{gathered} \right\}.\]
\label{lem:weak_top}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The main content of the argument is actually just checking $F$ is well-defined: through the cobar description we immediately get some $\Gamma$-module $\M$, but there is no immediate reason for the action to be continuous for the weak topology.

A priori, the $\Gamma$ action could be discontinuous for the weak topology. What we must check is that the coaction map
\[\M \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}) \otimes_{p_0, \mathrm{A}} \M \simeq \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)\]
is continuous for the weak topology on $\M$. This is really two claims: that the second isomorphism is an isomorphism of topological modules where $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ has the compact-open topology and $\M$ has the weak topology, and that the map is continuous. Once this is established the equivalence is clear, since the inverse to $F$ simply forgets all the topological data.

We will use the following general property of $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,-)$ with respect to exact sequences.

\begin{lemma}
Let $\mathrm{A}$ be complete Hausdorff metrizable, and let
\[0 \longrightarrow \mathrm{K} \longrightarrow \mathrm{A}^n \longrightarrow \M \longrightarrow 0\]
be an exact sequence of left modules where $\mathrm{A}^n$ has its natural product topology, $\mathrm{K}$ has the subspace topology and is closed, and $\M$ the quotient topology. Then
\[0 \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M) \longrightarrow 0\]
is a strictly exact sequence of topological modules over $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ where each is equipped with the compact-open topology.
\end{lemma}

Here the term ``strict exact'' means that the leftmost term has the subspace topology and the rightmost term has the quotient topology.

\begin{proof}
We first check $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n)$ is injective and acquires the subspace topology. For injectivity we may test this at the level of sets, where it is immediate since $\mathrm{K} \to \mathrm{A}^n$ is injective any function which is zero on $\mathrm{A}^n$ is necessarily zero on $\mathrm{K}$. Necessarily $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K})$ acquires the subspace topology, as a subbasis of opens are the collections $\V_{\Gamma',\U} = \{f \in \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K}): f(\Gamma')\subset \U\}$ where $\Gamma'\subseteq \Gamma$ is compact and $\U$ open. The subspace topology on the other hand asks for the same opens but where $\U \subseteq \mathrm{A}^n$ is open and we intersect with $\mathrm{K}$. Since $\mathrm{K}$ has the subspace topology we can match the subbases for the topology.

Middle exactness is also clear, as the functions sent to $0$ under $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$ are precisely those valued in $\mathrm{K}$. Thus the nontrivial content is surjectivity of $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$, and that the target acquires the quotient topology.

Using \cite[Theorem M, p. 86]{Wigner1973}, every continuous $f:\Gamma\to\M$ lifts to $f:\Gamma\to\mathrm{A}^n$ viewing both as additive topological groups. This proves surjectivity. We must also show that $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$ acquires the quotient topology, which is what we need for strictness. The map is continuous, so we must check $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$ is an open map.

Letting $\pi: \mathrm{A}^n \to \M$ denote the quotient map, by abuse of notation we also use $\pi$ for the map $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$. By virtue of being a homomorphism we must check $\pi_*(\V_{\Gamma,\U})=\V_{\Gamma,\pi(\U)}$ (in our previous notation for the subbasis of the compact-open topology; this is a basis around zero). More precisely we must check $f: \Gamma \to \pi(\U) \subset \M$ lifts to $\tilde{f}: \Gamma \to \U \subset \mathrm{A}^n$. Viewing $f$ as a map to $\M$ the previous result gives a lift, which need not land in $\U$. Around $\gamma \in \Gamma$ we may always correct this lift in an open neighborhood of $\gamma$ by taking $\tilde{f}-k_\gamma$, where $k_\gamma\in \mathrm{K}$. Since $\Gamma$ is profinite we can take a finite clopen partition into $\Gamma_i$ (not as subgroups!) so $\Gamma_i$ are contained in these opens, allowing us to correct $\tilde{f}$ piecewise by $k_{\gamma_i}$ to land in $\U$. This shows the claim.
\end{proof}

Granting the lemma the proof is straightforward. When $\M=\mathrm{A}^n$ the claim that $F$ is well-defined is clear. For general $\M$, consider the presentation $0 \to \mathrm{K} \to \mathrm{A}^n \twoheadrightarrow \M$. Since we assume the weak and subspace topologies on $\mathrm{K}$ are the same, it follows that $\mathrm{K} \subset \mathrm{A}^n$ is a complete additive subgroup hence closed (completeness follows from giving $\mathrm{K}$ the quotient topology from $\mathrm{A}^m \twoheadrightarrow \mathrm{K}$).

By the lemma we therefore get an exact sequence
\[0 \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M) \longrightarrow 0\]
and applying it again with $\mathrm{A}^m \twoheadrightarrow \mathrm{K}$ we get a right exact sequence
\[\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^m) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M) \longrightarrow 0.\]
For the first two we have $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}) \otimes_{p_0, \mathrm{A}} \mathrm{A}^n \simeq \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n)$ and similarly for $\mathrm{A}^m$, so keeping track of topologies we get an isomorphism of topological modules $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}) \otimes_{p_0, \mathrm{A}} \M \simeq \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$ where $\M$ has its weak topology.

Finally, continuity of $\M \to \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}) \otimes_{p_0, \mathrm{A}} \M$ is automatic from continuity of $\mathrm{A} \to \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$. The claim then follows.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
Let $\mathrm{A}$ be complete Hausdorff metrizable, and let
\[0 \longrightarrow \mathrm{K} \longrightarrow \mathrm{A}^n \longrightarrow \M \longrightarrow 0\]
be an exact sequence of left modules where $\mathrm{A}^n$ has its natural product topology, $\mathrm{K}$ has the subspace topology and is closed, and $\M$ the quotient topology. Then
\[0 \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M) \longrightarrow 0\]
is a strictly exact sequence of topological modules over $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A})$ where each is equipped with the compact-open topology.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We first check $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n)$ is injective and acquires the subspace topology. For injectivity we may test this at the level of sets, where it is immediate since $\mathrm{K} \to \mathrm{A}^n$ is injective any function which is zero on $\mathrm{A}^n$ is necessarily zero on $\mathrm{K}$. Necessarily $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K})$ acquires the subspace topology, as a subbasis of opens are the collections $\V_{\Gamma',\U} = \{f \in \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{K}): f(\Gamma')\subset \U\}$ where $\Gamma'\subseteq \Gamma$ is compact and $\U$ open. The subspace topology on the other hand asks for the same opens but where $\U \subseteq \mathrm{A}^n$ is open and we intersect with $\mathrm{K}$. Since $\mathrm{K}$ has the subspace topology we can match the subbases for the topology.

Middle exactness is also clear, as the functions sent to $0$ under $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$ are precisely those valued in $\mathrm{K}$. Thus the nontrivial content is surjectivity of $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$, and that the target acquires the quotient topology.

Using \cite[Theorem M, p. 86]{Wigner1973}, every continuous $f:\Gamma\to\M$ lifts to $f:\Gamma\to\mathrm{A}^n$ viewing both as additive topological groups. This proves surjectivity. We must also show that $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$ acquires the quotient topology, which is what we need for strictness. The map is continuous, so we must check $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$ is an open map.

Letting $\pi: \mathrm{A}^n \to \M$ denote the quotient map, by abuse of notation we also use $\pi$ for the map $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\mathrm{A}^n) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$. By virtue of being a homomorphism we must check $\pi_*(\V_{\Gamma,\U})=\V_{\Gamma,\pi(\U)}$ (in our previous notation for the subbasis of the compact-open topology; this is a basis around zero). More precisely we must check $f: \Gamma \to \pi(\U) \subset \M$ lifts to $\tilde{f}: \Gamma \to \U \subset \mathrm{A}^n$. Viewing $f$ as a map to $\M$ the previous result gives a lift, which need not land in $\U$. Around $\gamma \in \Gamma$ we may always correct this lift in an open neighborhood of $\gamma$ by taking $\tilde{f}-k_\gamma$, where $k_\gamma\in \mathrm{K}$. Since $\Gamma$ is profinite we can take a finite clopen partition into $\Gamma_i$ (not as subgroups!) so $\Gamma_i$ are contained in these opens, allowing us to correct $\tilde{f}$ piecewise by $k_{\gamma_i}$ to land in $\U$. This shows the claim.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
Let $s=1$ or $2$. For every finite $\overline{\mathrm{A}}$-module $\mathrm{N}$, the map $\theta_s$ induces an injection
\[\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\mathrm{N} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{N}).\]
If $\M \subset \mathrm{N}$ is a finite submodule stable under $\Gamma^s$, then inside $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{N})$ one further has
\[\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\M = \bigl(\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\mathrm{N}\bigr) \cap\mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\M).\]
\label{lem:Cech_finite_coefficients}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The first claim is straightforward using the basis $\eta_{\alpha}$ from Definition \ref{def:Cq}. An element $f\in \overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\mathrm{N}$ has an expansion
\[f=\sum_{\alpha\in\N^{s(n+1)}}m_\alpha \eta_\alpha.\]
Just as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:Cq_criterion} for $\alpha,\ell\in\N^{s(n+1)}$ we have $\eta_\alpha(\ell)=0$ unless $\alpha \leq \ell$ coordinatewise, while $\eta_\ell(\ell)\in\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{\times}$. If $f$ evaluates to zero, then for the remaining terms we get
\[0=f(\ell)=\sum_{\alpha\leq\ell}m_\alpha \eta_\alpha(\ell).\]
This sum is finite. Induction on $|\ell|$ therefore gives $m_\ell=0$ for every $\ell$, proving injectivity.

We now attack the second claim, namely that if $\M\subset\mathrm{N}$ is a finite stable under $\Gamma^s$, then
\[\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\M = \bigl(\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\mathrm{N}\bigr) \cap\mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\M).\] 
It is useful to observe that the map $p_0:\mathrm{A}\to\mathrm{A}^{(s)}$ is $p$-completely flat: before applying $(-)[1/[p]_q]_p^{\wedge}$ we see $(p,[p]_q)$-complete flatness follows from flatness of prismatic envelopes (see \cite[Proposition 5.52]{MaoDerivedCrystalline}). Since $\mathrm{A}^+$ is Noetherian, \cite[Lemma 5.15]{BhattCohenMacaulayAIC} makes $p_0:\mathrm{A}\to\mathrm{A}^{(s)}$ $p$-completely flat as it is the $p$-completion of a flat map. Its reduction modulo $p$, $p_0:\overline{\mathrm{A}}\to\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}$, is then flat.

Consider now the commutative square
\begin{display}
\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\mathrm{N} \ar{r} \ar{d} & \mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{N}) \ar{d} \\
\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\mathrm{N}/\M) \ar{r} & \mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{N}/\M).
\end{display}
The lower horizontal map is injective by the first claim of the lemma. Flatness identifies the kernel of the left vertical map with $\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\M$. If an element of the upper left term $\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\mathrm{N}$ maps into $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\M)$, its image in the lower right term $\mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\mathrm{N}/\M)$ vanishes. It therefore vanishes in the lower left term $\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}(\mathrm{N}/\M)$ and belongs to $\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\M$ (using injectivity of the lower horizontal map). Thus 
\[\bigl(\overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\mathrm{N}\bigr)\cap\mathrm{C}(\Gamma^s,\M) \subseteq \overline{\mathrm{A}}^{(s)}\otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\M.\]
The reverse inclusion is clear since $\M \subset \mathrm{N}$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
Let $\M$ be a finite $\overline{\mathrm{A}}$-module with continuous semilinear $\Gamma$-action. For $k\gg0$, the coaction of $\varphi^{*k}\M$ factors through
\[\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}}) \otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}}\varphi^{*k}\M \subset \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\varphi^{*k} \M).\]
The same holds with $\Gamma^2$ as needed for the cocycle condition.
\label{lem:Gamma_Frob_improvement}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
We explain the proof for $\Gamma$, as the argument for $\Gamma^2$ is similar. In Lemma \ref{lem:Cq_criterion} we can immediately adapt it with coefficients to give a criterion for membership in $\mathrm{C}_q(\Gamma,\overline{\mathrm{A}}) \otimes_{\overline{\mathrm{A}},p_0}^{\mathord{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.75}{$\displaystyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\textstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptstyle\blacksquare$}}{\scalebox{0.75}{$\scriptscriptstyle\blacksquare$}}}} \M \subset \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$ in terms of how rapidly Mahler coefficients tend to zero. Here to make sense of the target we have equipped $\M$ with its weak topology.

For $f\in \mathrm{C}(\Gamma,\M)$, take its Mahler expansion
\[f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in \N^{n+1}} m_\alpha\binom{x}{\alpha},\]
where $\binom{x}{\alpha}=\prod_i\binom{x_i}{\alpha_i}$. The desired criterion is then that if there are $\sigma>1$ and $\mathrm{C}$ for which
